source_text: Καὶ τάχα οὐκ ἐλάττων ὁ κίνδυνος τῷ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἃ μὴ χρὴ κατάγοντι, ἤπερ τῷ τὰ κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον ὀνόματα ἐναλλάσσοντι καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ τῶν ἐλαττόνων φέροντι ἐπὶ τὰ κρείττονα τὰ δὲ κατὰ τῶν κρειττόνων ἐπὶ τὰ ἥττονα. καὶ οὐ λέγω ὅτι τῷ Διῒ εὐθέως συνεξακούεται ὁ Κρόνου καὶ Ῥέας υἱὸς καὶ Ἥρας ἀνὴρ καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος πατὴρ καὶ ὁ τῇ θυγατρὶ Περσεφόνῃ μιγεὶς, ἢ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι συνεξακούεται ὁ Λητοῦς καὶ Διὸς υἱὸς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἑρμοῦ ὁμοπάτριος ἀδελφὸς, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα φέρουσιν οἱ σοφοὶ Κέλσου τῶν δογμάτων πατέρες καὶ ἀρχαῖοι θεολόγοι Ἑλλήνων. τίς γὰρ ἡ ἀποκλήρωσις, κυριολεκτεῖσθαι μὲν τὸν Δία οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν πατέρα μὲν αὐτοῦ εἶναι Κρόνον μητέρα δὲ Ῥέαν; τὸ δ᾿ ὅμοιον ποιητέον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὀνομαζομένων θεῶν. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἔγκλημα οὐδαμῶς ἅπτεται τῶν κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον τὸ Σαβαὼθ τασσόντων ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ Ἀδωναῒ ἤ τι τῶν λοιπῶν ὀνομάτων. ὅταν δὲ τὰ περὶ ὀνομάτων τις δύνηται τὰ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις φιλοσοφεῖν, πολλὰ ἂν εὕροι καὶ περὶ τῆς ἐπικλήσεως τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ· ὧν ὁ μέν τις Μιχαὴλ ἕτερος δὲ Γαβριὴλ καὶ ἄλλος Ῥαφαὴλ καλεῖται. φερωνύμως τοῖς πράγμασιν, ἃ διακονοῦνται κατὰ βούλημα τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἐν τῷ παντί. τῆς δ᾿ ὁμοίας ἔχεται περὶ ὀνομάτων φιλοσοφίας καὶ ὁ ἡμέτερος Ἰησοῦς, οὗ τὸ ὄνομα μυρίους ἤδη ἐναργῶς ἑώραται δαίμονας ἐξελάσαν ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων, ἐνεργῆσαν εἰς ἐκείνους ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἀπηλάθησαν. ἔτι δ᾿ εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον λεκτέον ὅτι οἱ περὶ τὴν χρῆσιν τῶν ἐπῳδῶν δεινοὶ ἱστοροῦσιν, ὅτι τὴν αὐτὴν ἐπῳδὴν εἰπόντα μὲν τῇ οἰκείᾳ διαλέκτῳ ἔστιν ἐνεργῆσαι ὅπερ ἐπαγγέλλεται ἡ ἐπῳδή· μεταλαβόντα δὲ εἰς ἄλλην οἱανδηποτοῦν φωνὴν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἄτονον καὶ οὐδὲν δυναμένην. οὕτως οὐ τὰ σημαινόμενα κατὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἀλλ᾿ αἱ τῶν φωνῶν ποιότητες καὶ ἰδιότητες ἔχουσί τι δυνατὸν ἐν αὐταῖς πρὸς τάδε τινὰ ἢ τάδε. οὕτω δ᾿ ἀπολογησόμεθα διὰ τῶν τοιούτων καὶ περὶ τοῦ μέχρι θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι Χριστιανοὺς, ἵνα μὴ τὸν Δία θεὸν ἀναγορεύσωσι μηδ᾿ ἄλλῃ διαλέκτῳ αὐτὸν ὀνομάσωσιν. ἢ γὰρ ἀορίστως ὁμολογοῦσι τὸ κοινὸν ὄνομα τὸ θεὸς ἢ καὶ μετὰ προσθήκης τῆς·“ ὁ δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων, ὁ ποιητὴς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὁ καταπέμψας τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς σοφούς“· ὡς τῷ ὀνόματι ἐφαρμοζόμενον τὸ θεὸς ὄνομα δύναμίν τινα παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἐπιτελεῖ. πολλὰ δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἄλλα λέγοιτο εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον πρὸς τοὺς οἰομένους δεῖν ἀδιαφορεῖν περὶ τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν. καὶ εἴπερ θαυμάζεται Πλάτων εἰπὼν ἐν Φιλήβῳ· „τὸ δ᾿ ἐμὸν δέος, ὦ Πρώταρχε. περὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν θεῶν οὐκ ὀλίγον.“ ἐπεὶ Φίληβος θεὸν τὴν ἡδονὴν εἶπεν ὁ προσδιαλεγόμενος τῷ Σωκράτει· πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον τῆς εὐλαβείας ἀποδεξόμεθα Χριστιανοὺς, μηδὲν τῶν ἐν ταῖς μυθοποιΐαις παραλαμβανομένων ὀνομάτων προσάπτοντας τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ; ἀλλὰ γὰρ τούτων ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἅλις.
pass_a_gloss: And perhaps the danger is not less for the one who brings down the name of God or the name of the good upon things which they should not, than for the one who exchanges names which are unspeakable and some of which are brought from lesser things to greater things and some from greater things to lesser things. And I do not say that to Zeus is immediately heard the son of Cronus and Rhea and the husband of Hera and the brother of Poseidon and the father of Athena and Artemis and the one who had intercourse with his daughter Persephone, or that to Apollo is heard the son of Leto and Zeus and the brother of Artemis and the brother of Hermes, and the other things which the wise men of Celsus, the fathers of doctrines and the ancient theologians of the Greeks, bring. For what is the explanation, to speak literally of Zeus, but not also that his father is Cronus and his mother is Rhea? And one must do the same thing also concerning the other named gods. But this accusation does not touch at all those who assign the name Sabaoth to God or the name Adonai or any of the other names. When someone is able to philosophize about the things concerning names which are in the unspeakable things, they will find many things also concerning the invocation of the angels of God, of whom one is called Michael and another Gabriel and another Raphael. They are named in relation to the things which they serve according to the will of God of all things in the universe. And our Jesus also holds the same philosophy concerning names, whose name has already been clearly seen to cast out myriads of demons from souls and bodies, and to work upon those from whom they were cast out. And yet, concerning the place of names, it must be said that those who are skilled in the use of incantations tell that the same incantation, when spoken in its own dialect, is able to accomplish what it promises, but when it is translated into any other language, it is seen to be weak and unable to do anything. Thus, it is not the things signified in relation to the things, but the qualities and properties of the sounds that have some power in them for certain things. Thus, we will apologize through such things also concerning the Christians who struggle until death, so that they may not proclaim Zeus as God nor name him in any other language. For either they confess the common name God without distinction or also with the addition of 'the creator of all things, the maker of heaven and earth, the one who sent to the race of men these certain wise men', as if the name God, when applied, accomplishes some power among men. Many other things could also be said concerning the place of names to those who think that they should be indifferent to the use of them. And if Plato is admired for saying in Philebus, 'My fear, O Protarchus, is not small concerning the names of the gods', since Philebus said that God is pleasure, the one who converses with Socrates, how much more will we accept the reverence of Christians, who do not apply any of the names taken from myths to the creator of the universe? But enough of these things for now.

pass_b_english: The danger may well be no smaller for someone who drags the name of God, or the name of the Good, down onto things where it does not belong, than for someone who swaps the unspeakable names — shifting some from lesser realities up to greater ones, and others from greater realities down to lesser ones. I am not claiming that the moment the name Zeus is spoken, one immediately hears along with it the son of Cronus and Rhea, the husband of Hera, the brother of Poseidon, the father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who lay with his own daughter Persephone; nor that the name Apollo summons the son of Leto and Zeus, the brother of Artemis, the half-brother of Hermes, and whatever other titles the wise men of Celsus — fathers of doctrines and ancient theologians of the Greeks — attach to them. For what is the definition, if we speak literally of Zeus, that does not also include his father being Cronus and his mother Rhea? The same must be done for every other named god. Yet this charge does not touch at all those who assign the name Sabaoth to God, or Adonai, or any of the other names. When someone can philosophize about names as they exist in the unspeakable realm, they will discover many things also about the invocation of God's angels — one called Michael, another Gabriel, another Raphael — named in relation to the tasks they perform by the will of the God of all things throughout the universe. Our Jesus shares this same philosophy of names: his name has already been seen clearly to cast out myriads of demons from souls and bodies, and to work powerfully upon those from whom the demons were driven. Further, on the subject of names, it must be said that those skilled in the use of incantations report that the same incantation, when spoken in its own dialect, can accomplish what it promises; but when translated into any other language, it is seen to be feeble and unable to do anything. Thus it is not the meanings attached to things, but the qualities and properties of the sounds themselves, that possess some power for certain effects. So we will defend ourselves by such reasoning also concerning Christians who struggle to the death rather than proclaim Zeus as God or name him in any other tongue. For they either confess the common name God without qualification, or with the addition: "the creator of all things, the maker of heaven and earth, the one who sent to the race of men these certain wise men" — as if the name God, when invoked, accomplishes some power among human beings. Many other things could be said on the subject of names to those who think they should be indifferent to their use. And if Plato is admired for saying in the Philebus, "My fear, Protarchus, concerning the names of the gods is not small" — since Philebus had declared pleasure to be god, the one conversing with Socrates — how much more will we accept the reverence of Christians, who attach none of the names taken from myths to the creator of the universe? But enough of these things for now.
